name: Spacemen 3

place.note: Same lineage as spiritualized (Jason Pierce's later band). Alt: american-underground/neo-psych is wrong place (they are Rugby, England). No scene: not in a shared room with any scene on the list.

edges.found: The big thing for me, that I took from The Velvet Underground into Spacemen 3, was the drone.
edges.citation: Sonic Boom (Peter Kember), MOJO: "The big thing for me, that I took from The Velvet Underground into Spacemen 3, was the drone."

edges.found: I think that's something we got from the Stooges, "O.D. Catastrophe"…
edges.citation: Sonic Boom to Forced Exposure, September 1988, on the band's one-chord, twenty-minute concentration: "I think that's something we got from the Stooges, 'O.D. Catastrophe'."
edges.note: Page is a fan-run archive (spacemen3.co.uk) of the original zine interview; ledger.ts read OK. Context sentence before it: 'saying it's all one chord belittles the song'.

edges.found: We do a song called "Suicide" which we dedicate to them every gig. It's kind of like Suicide and the Stooges crossed. It's got keyboards and the drummer drums like Martin Rev's right hand.
edges.citation: Sonic Boom to Forced Exposure, September 1988: "We do a song called 'Suicide' which we dedicate to them every gig. It's kind of like Suicide and the Stooges crossed."
edges.note: Dedicated tribute rather than the word 'influence'; same page also has him admitting they got the Suicide sound partly from the Stooges. Acceptable as first-person fan/tribute, owner may rule.

edges.found: I certainly think it owes more to Sun Ra than MC5, but it does definitely owe a fair bit to the MC5. When we do that song live, we tend to do it more like the MC5 version.
edges.citation: Sonic Boom to Forced Exposure, September 1988, on the band's own version of "Starship": "it does definitely owe a fair bit to the MC5."
edges.note: About one song (a cover of MC5's Starship); weaker. Cover-adjacent trap, so only include if owner is generous.

edges.found: all around us, in the air, it seemed, were bands that came a bit before us, like My Bloody Valentine, Spacemen 3, and Loop. They had a noise element that we found really cool.
edges.citation: Ride's Andy Bell, Premier Guitar: "bands that came a bit before us, like My Bloody Valentine, Spacemen 3, and Loop. They had a noise element that we found really cool."
edges.note: Also Quietus Baker's Dozen (Bell, page 4): Spacemen 3 poster on his wall, listening to The Perfect Prescription (1987) while Ride was forming 1988. Supports it.

edges.found: Some of the bands we were inspired by—Spacemen 3, Joy Division, the Cure, Velvet Underground. They all had a little bit of a minimalist end to their spectrum, maybe some quieter songs that we thought, "What if everything was like that?"
edges.citation: Low, in The Current's "Low: 25 Years In" (2019): "Some of the bands we were inspired by—Spacemen 3, Joy Division, the Cure, Velvet Underground."
edges.note: I did not confirm which member's words these are (page is Low's own retrospective text); band speaking as 'we'.

edges.found: Then they started playing 'Revolution' [from 1989's Playing With Fire], first as an instrumental, and then with the lyrics, and that just became an anthem for me and my friends, our generation of psychedelic warriors. Sonic would send me mixtapes. This was my other gateway after David Bowie and the Velvets. He introduced me to Suicide, The Beach Boys, 13th Floor Elevators, Tav Falco's Panther Burns, Red Krayola, all of these things that I'd never heard of but that became really important for me.
edges.citation: Pulp's Mark Webber, Quietus Baker's Dozen: Sonic Boom "introduced me to Suicide, The Beach Boys, 13th Floor Elevators... all of these things that I'd never heard of but that became really important for me."
edges.note: HOLD / owner ruling. Real formative fandom (organised their gig at 16), but Webber joined Pulp ~1980s and says nothing about Pulp's music being shaped. Judge: favourite/contested. Also the real edge (Webber -> Suicide/Velvets via Sonic) is off-map-mediated.

rejected.why: Britt Daniel (Quietus): loves The Perfect Prescription, found it in high school; nothing about shaping Spoon. Favourite only.
Simeon Coxe praises the Threebie EP; Silver Apples formed 1967, 20 years earlier. Favourite and backwards in time.
Personnel (Jason Pierce). No edge from membership; Spiritualized's own words about Spacemen 3 would need a separate source.
Not on the map. Sonic Boom discusses their Rollercoaster in the same Forced Exposure page (they adapted it); could be an edge if the owner adds the Elevators.

Sonic denies the Mary Chain comparison: 'We were going for years before the Mary Chain even started... I didn't quite listen to Psychocandy for at least a year after that.' Not on a denial list of anyone on map? JAMC is on the map, so this is a clean-ish denial of the critic comparison (see denials note).
Search-summary-level lists (Wikipedia influences, fan-wiki MC5/Beefheart/Kraftwerk). Not used as sources.

content.bio:
Spacemen 3 formed in Rugby, England in 1982 around two friends, Peter Kember (Sonic Boom) and Jason Pierce. They played long, hypnotic songs built from one or two chords, repeated until they hit a trance, with fuzz guitar, tremolo and a lot of volume. Their model was the Velvet Underground, the Stooges and Suicide, and they used the stage as a place to play it rather than perform it.

Their records made the idea quieter and stranger. The Perfect Prescription (1987) is laid out like a single comedown, from big fuzzy songs to hushed, gentle ones, and Playing with Fire (1989) went further into slow, wide-open psychedelia. The two writers fell out and the band split in 1991, Kember going on to Spectrum and Pierce to Spiritualized. Their drone-and-tremolo sound became a reference point for the bands that followed, from Ride and Low to Spoon.

album.title: The Perfect Prescription
album.classicReason: A record structured like a night out followed by the comedown, it swings between loud, fuzzy songs and hushed, acoustic ones. "Walkin' with Jesus" and "Come Down Easy" show the band's trick of one repeating figure and slowly shifting tremolo. It remains the clearest account of how drone could be made gentle as well as heavy, and bands like Ride and Low have named it.
